flagged.title: Context: 1981 Britain, Race & the Care System
flagged.reason: The video attributes a completely fabricated dedication quotation to the novel ('For all the brothers and sisters who were separated') and presents invented police raids on Black businesses as the trigger for the Handsworth riots.

mark_affecting.quote: It was a powder keg sparked by three main things: aggressive police raids on Black-owned businesses and homes... For two whole days, there was intense violence
look at the dedication at the very beginning of the book. It says, 'For all the brothers and sisters who were separated.'

flagged.title: Part 2: Foster Care & Maureen
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly presents ongoing contact visits with Jake instead of Carol, misattributes the allotment to Maureen's garden, and completely misidentifies Maureen as a Jamaican British foster carer providing Black cultural connection when she is white.

mark_affecting.quote: Maureen's Garden: Nurture vs Impermanence... Maureen's garden has a really profound duality to it.

At first, the visits are joyful. Agonising, yes, because Leon has to sit there and watch his baby brother changing and growing without him... the gaps between the visits deliberately start to stretch out

mark_affecting.video_says: Enter Maureen. She is a Jamaican British foster carer... She gives Leon this absolutely crucial connection to his Black heritage, by cooking Caribbean food and speaking with a Jamaican dialect, she normalises his mixed-race identity
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Maureen is a white British woman... She cannot give Leon a link to his Black heritage, though. He finds that later, with Tufty and the men at the allotments — the diaspora community the white care system never offers him. Cultural identity: Maureen is white, so she cannot give Leon a link to his Black heritage.

flagged.title: Part 3: The Riots & the Ending
flagged.reason: The video states that Leon is settled at Maureen's in Part 3, whereas Maureen is hospitalized and Leon is staying with Sylvia when he searches for Jake and gets caught in the riots.

mark_affecting.quote: We've got Leon physically settled at Maureen's, but completely consumed by his secret mission to find baby Jake.

flagged.title: Character Analysis
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly describes Maureen as a Jamaican-British foster mother who provides Leon with cultural connection, directly contradicting the lesson and text where Maureen is white and unable to provide a link to his Black heritage.

mark_affecting.video_says: the Jamaican-British foster mother... offers... a vital cultural connection for Leon
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Maureen is white... What she cannot give him is a link to his Black heritage.

flagged.title: Structure, Narration & Voice
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims De Waal shifts into the present tense for emotional intensity when the entire novel is in present tense, and falsely claims Leon's race is rarely stated explicitly when he directly discusses it on page one.

mark_affecting.quote: De Waal also shifts into the present tense during moments of high emotional intensity, to drag us right into the moment.
Leon's race is rarely stated explicitly. You kind of figure it out based on how the world responds to him.

flagged.title: Key Themes
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly attributes cultural anchoring and introducing Leon to Caribbean food, music, and community to Maureen (his white foster carer) rather than Tufty, a major character and plot error that would lose marks in an exam.

mark_affecting.video_says: De Waal uses her [Maureen] to throw Leon a vital lifeline. It's a concept called cultural anchoring. Maureen gives Leon access to Caribbean food, music, and community. She essentially shows us what culturally competent care actually looks like...
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Tufty provides the cultural anchoring that the care system and Leon’s white carers cannot. Through Tufty and the allotment men, Leon gains access to Caribbean food, music, language, and community... Leon is placed with white carers, so De Waal gives him Tufty instead — a Black father figure who supplies what the placement cannot.
